narrative:
You were denied a promotion because the model predicted a 61% probability that you will leave your job. In other words, the model believes you are more likely than not to depart, making a promotion a risky investment for the organization.

The strongest factor driving this prediction is that you have received other job opportunities while in your current role. Only about 23% of employees predicted to stay have such opportunities, so this strongly pushes the model toward “will leave.” The second most influential factor is the amount of training you attended in the last three years: you completed 1–3 programs, which is roughly average among stayers (about 33% had none, 33% had 1–3), yet this still contributed positively to the leaving prediction. Third, your years of experience—6–10 years both overall and in your current job—also pushed toward leaving; among stayers, only about 35% have this level of experience, while half have 1–5 years.

Given these signals, the organization should consider discussing your career intentions and development. If you intend to stay, clearly communicate that and ask what specific steps would strengthen your case for promotion. The organization might also review whether additional training or clearer advancement paths could reduce the likelihood of you leaving.
